paras: The killing of the Laurant family was the shooting of four Black men of one family, and the wounding of two others, by white men at a logging settlement near Florenville in St. Tammany Parish, Louisiana, on May 9, 1903. The trouble was traced to a white store clerk striking one of the family with an axe handle for failing to address him respectfully. Wire services reported it across the country as a "race riot" or "pitched battle," and the deputies who arrived afterward were reported to have arrested only Black men.

The settlement stood at the end of a logging road running from the East Louisiana railroad at Florenville toward Pearl River, about twenty miles from Covington, where many Black men cut logs. P. H. Hansborough, general superintendent of the Poitevent & Favre Company's logging interests, kept a store there, with a young man from Mississippi as clerk.

Several days before the killings, according to the parish paper, one of the sons became "fresh" with the clerk, calling him by his last name without courtesy, and the clerk knocked him down with an axe handle. Soon afterward the injured man received a load of shot from someone near the store whom the paper did not identify. The same account described the family as "sulky and impudent," said they had obtained firearms and practiced at a target, and reported remarks about what might happen if whites said anything.

On Saturday, May 9, the parish paper wrote, "the leading white men of the settlement" took the matter into their own hands, "tiring of the insulting manner of the blacks." A burst of gunfire followed into Saturday night, killing three members of the family outright; a fourth died before officers arrived, and two others were wounded. No white casualties were reported.

Deputy sheriffs Hiram Cook and S. J. Talley reached the scene after quiet had been restored. The parish paper reported a single arrest, Jules Laurant, on a charge of assault and battery, while the New Orleans report said two or three "ringleaders who had escaped the vengeance of the citizens" were in jail at Covington. Coroner F. Julius Heintz held the inquests on Monday morning, May 11, but no verdict appears in the coverage, and no report of any white man being arrested or charged was found.

The Associated Press sent a brief New Orleans dispatch on May 11 describing an "insolent negro," Black men who "armed and sought to cause trouble," and a pitched battle in which four of the "Florant family," one of them "the aggressor," were killed. Southern papers ran it under headlines such as "A NEGRO UPRISING. They Sought to Fight In Louisiana and Four Passed to the Beyond" in Birmingham, "FOUR NEGROES KILLED IN A RACE BATTLE" in Savannah, and "A Race War Soon Over" in Pickens, South Carolina. Two South Carolina weeklies garbled it into a riot "in New Orleans."

A fuller New Orleans account, apparently from the Picayune, ran in the Paducah Sun under the deck "The Whites Had Tired of Their Impa dence" and was repeated almost word for word by the St. Tammany Farmer under "Fatal Shooting Affray." The New York Sun's version said a party of white men had tried to disarm the family, and its headline read "Negroes Shot Dead in a Lumber Camp for an Insult to a White Man." Two weeks later the Farmer corrected the Picayune's placement of the killing in the Parker Settlement, saying it occurred several miles below.
The only Black-press item found, in the Cleveland Gazette of May 16, reprinted the AP paragraph, "little race riot" and "insolent negro" included, in a news-summary column without comment.

All accounts come from white sources, and they differ on how the shooting began: the local paper said white men took matters into their own hands, the New York Sun said whites tried to disarm armed Black men, and the AP described a pitched battle the Black men started. The family name appears as Laurant in the parish paper, Larton or Lorant in the New Orleans report, and Florant in the AP; the local form is supported by its naming of Jules Laurant.

reader.title: Killing of the Laurant family near Florenville, Louisiana
bases: Four members of one Black family were shot dead and two wounded by white men of a logging settlement who, in the local paper's words, 'took the matter in their own hands' after a Black man's alleged disrespect to a white clerk; the wire called it a race riot or pitched battle (A1, A11, A4).

The local and New Orleans accounts say 'the leading white men of the settlement' took the matter into their own hands, tired of the 'insulting manner of the blacks', and killed four before officers arrived (A11, A1); the AP version instead describes Black men arming and a 'pitched battle', so the killings may have been framed as a fight, and every account comes from the white side (A4, A6).

The AP dispatch and the separate New Orleans (Picayune-derived) report, repeated by the parish paper, agree that four members of one Black family were killed by whites in a St. Tammany logging settlement after a clerk struck one of them with an axe handle (A2, A1, A11, A6).

accounts.label: New Orleans report (Picayune-derived) and parish paper
accounts.gist: After a clerk struck a Laurant son for disrespect and the son was later shot by an unknown person, the family armed and grew 'impudent'; tired of this, the leading white men of the settlement took matters into their own hands and killed four.

accounts.label: New York Sun dispatch
accounts.gist: The Lorants and other Black men armed after the axe-handle blow; a party of white men undertook to disarm them, shots were fired, and four were killed.

accounts.label: Associated Press brief
accounts.gist: An 'insolent negro' was beaten by a white grocery clerk; the Black men armed 'and sought to cause trouble', the whites rallied, and a pitched battle left four Black men dead, one of them 'the aggressor'.

framing.detail: The parish paper and the Paducah Sun described the family as 'obnoxious', 'sulky and impudent' and explained the killing by the whites' tiring of 'the insulting manner of the blacks'; the Paducah deck read 'The Whites Had Tired of Their Impa[ti]dence'.
The AP brief ran under headlines such as 'A NEGRO UPRISING', 'FOUR NEGROES KILLED IN A RACE BATTLE' and 'A Race War Soon Over', closing that 'the trouble is over'.
The New York Sun headed its dispatch 'Negroes Shot Dead in a Lumber Camp for an Insult to a White Man', putting the cause in the insult.
The Cleveland Gazette reprinted the AP paragraph, including 'a little race riot' and 'insolent negro', in a news-summary column without comment.
